segments.heading: Introduction
segments.text: The most peculiar and firm principle, says Proclus, of all the dialogues of Plato, and of the whole theory of that philosopher, is the knowledge of our own nature; for, this being properly established as an hypothesis, we shall be able accurately to learn the good which is adapted to us, and the evil which opposes this good. For, as the essences of things are different, so also are their proper perfections; and this according to a subjection of essence. For, whether being and the good proceed, as Aristotle says, from the same Vesta and first fountain, it is certainly necessary that perfection should be imparted to every thing according to the measures of essence; or whether good proceeds from a cause more ancient and more characterized by unity, but essence and being are imparted to things from another cause; still, as every thing participates of being more obscurely and more clearly, in the same degree must it participate of good; first beings, in a greater and more perfect manner; but those that rank in the middle orders, secondarily; and the last of things according to an ultimate subsistence. For, how otherwise can things participate of deity and providence, and a distribution according to their desert? For it must not be admitted that intellect can lead things into order, and impart to each a convenient measure, but that the good, or the ineffable principle of things, which is more ancient than intellect, should make its communications in a disordered manner; viz. that it should impart to causes and things caused the same portion of goodness, and distribute to the same things according to being the perfections of more primary and subordinate natures. For it neither was lawful, says Timæus, nor is, for the best of natures to effect any thing but that which is most beautiful and most commensurate. But the same good is not most commensurate to first and secondary natures; but, as the Athenian guest says, a distribution of inequality to things unequal, and of equality to things equal, of the greater to such as are greater, and of the lesser to such as are lesser, is of all things the most musical and the best.

segments.heading: Introduction
segments.text: According to this reasoning, therefore, good is different in different beings, and a certain good is naturally co-ordinated to the essence of every thing. Hence the perfection of intellect is in eternity, but of the rational soul in time: and the good of the rational soul consists in an energy according to intellect, but the good of body is in a subsistence according to nature; so that he who thinks that though the nature in these is different, yet the perfection is the same, has an erroneous conception of the truth of things.

segments.heading: Introduction
segments.text: According to every order of beings, therefore, essence ought to be known prior to perfection; for perfection is not of itself, but of essence, by which it is participated. Hence, with respect to the essence of a thing, we must first consider whether it belongs to impartible essences, such as intellectual natures, or to such as are divisible about bodies, viz. corporeal forms and qualities, or to such as subsist between these. Likewise, whether it ranks among eternal entities, or such as subsist according to the whole of time, or such as are generated in a certain part of time. Again, whether it is simple, and subsists prior to composition, or is indeed a composite, but is always in the act of being bound with indissoluble bonds, or may again be resolved into those things from which it is composed. For, by thus considering every thing, we shall be able to understand in what its good consists. For, again, it is evident that the good of those natures which are allotted an impartible essence is eternal, but that the good of partible natures is conversant with time and motion; and that the good of things subsisting between these is to be considered according to the measures of subsistence and perfection; viz. that such a nature is indeed indigent of time, but of first time, which is able to measure incorporeal periods. So that the pure and genuine knowledge of ourselves, circumscribed in scientific boundaries, must, as we have said, be considered as the most proper principle of all philosophy, and of the doctrine of Plato. For, where is it proper to begin, except from the purification and perfection of ourselves, and whence the Delphic god exhorts us to begin? For, as those who enter the Eleusinian grove are ordered by an inscription not to enter into the adyta of the temple, if they are uninitiated in the highest of the mysteries, so the inscription KNOW THYSELF, on the Delphic temple, manifests, as it appears to me, the mode of returning to a divine nature, and the most useful path to purification, all but perspicuously asserting to the intelligent, that he who knows himself beginning from the Vestal hearth may be able to be conjoined with that divinity who unfolds into light the whole of truth, and is the leader of a cathartic life; but that he who is ignorant of himself, as being uninitiated both in the lesser and greater mysteries, is unadapted to participate the providence of Apollo. Hence then let us also begin conformably to the mandate of the god, and let us investigate in which of his dialogues Plato especially makes the speculation of our essence his principal design, that from hence we may also make the commencement of the Platonic writing. Can we then adduce any other writing of Plato except the first Alcibiades, and the conference of Socrates which is delivered in this dialogue? Where else shall we say our essence is so unfolded? Where besides are man and the nature of man investigated? To which we may add, that it is Socrates who engages in this first conversation with Alcibiades, and that it is he who says that the beginning of perfection is suspended from the contemplation of ourselves. For we are ignorant of ourselves in consequence of being involved in oblivion produced by the realms of generation, and agitated by the tumult of the irrational forms of life. In the mean time, we think that we know many things of which we are ignorant, because we essentially possess innate reasons of things.

segments.heading: Introduction
segments.text: This dialogue therefore is the beginning of all philosophy, in the same manner as the knowledge of ourselves. Hence many logical and ethical theorems are scattered in it, together with such as contribute to the entire speculation of felicity. It likewise contains information with respect to many things which contribute to physiology, and to those dogmas which lead us to the truth concerning divine natures themselves. Hence too the divine Iamblichus assigned this dialogue the first rank, in the ten dialogues, in which he was of opinion the whole philosophy of Plato was contained.

segments.heading: Introduction
segments.text: Of the particulars exhibited in this dialogue, some precede and others follow the principal design, which is the knowledge of ourselves. For the hypothesis of two-fold ignorance, exhortation, and the like precede; but the demonstration of virtue and felicity, and the rejection of the multitude of arts, as being ignorant of themselves, of things pertaining to themselves, and in short of all things,—and every thing else of this kind, have a consequent order. But the most perfect and leading design of the whole conversation is the speculation of our own essence. So that he will not err who establishes the care and knowledge of ourselves, as the end of the dialogue.

segments.heading: Introduction
segments.text: Again, the amatory form of life is particularly indicated by Socrates in this dialogue. For the beginning is made from hence; and he proceeds perfecting the young man till he renders him a lover of his providential care, which is the leading good of the amatory art. And in short, through all the divisions of the dialogue, he always preserves that which is adapted to an amatory life. As there are three sciences, then, which Socrates appears to have testified that he possessed, viz. the dialectic, the maieutic, (i.e. obstetric,) and the amatory, we shall find the form of the dialectic and the peculiarity of the maieutic science in this dialogue, but the effects of the amatory science predominate in it. For, when Socrates is calling forth the conceptions of Alcibiades, he still acts conformably to the amatory character; and when he employs the dialectic science, he does not depart from the peculiarity of amatory arguments. Just as in the Theætetus he is maieutic, is principally characterized according to this, and proceeds as far as to a purification of the same opinions of Theætetus: but, having effected this, he dismisses him, as being now able of himself to know the truth, which is the business of the maieutic science, as he himself asserts in that dialogue. Thus also he first indicates the amatory science in this dialogue, with which both the dialectic and maieutic are mingled. For every where Socrates introduces discourses adapted to the subject persons. And as every kind of good pre-subsists in a divine nature, which is variously possessed by different beings according to the natural aptitude of each, in like manner Socrates, who comprehends all sciences in himself, employs a different science at different times, according to the aptitude of the recipients; elevating one through the amatory science; exciting another to the reminiscence of the eternal reasons of the soul through the maieutic science; and conducting another according to the dialectic method to the speculation of beings. Some too he conjoins to the beautiful itself, others to the first wisdom, and others to the good itself. For through the amatory science we are led to the beautiful; through the maieutic, by calling forth our latent reasons, we become wise in things of which we were ignorant; and through the dialectic science we ascend as far as to the good.

segments.heading: Introduction
segments.text: Lastly, it will be found by those who are deeply skilled in the philosophy of Plato, that each of his dialogues contains that which the universe contains. Hence, in every dialogue, one thing is analogous to the good, another to intellect, another to soul, another to form, and another to matter. In this dialogue therefore it must be said, that an assimilation to a divine nature is analogous to the good; the knowledge of ourselves to intellect; the multitude of the demonstrations leading us to the conclusion, and in short every thing syllogistic in the dialogue, to soul; the character of the diction, and whatever else pertains to the power of speech, to form; and the persons, the occasion, and that which is called by rhetoricians the hypothesis, to matter.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text:
PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE:
SOCRATES, ALCIBIADES.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SCENE, (most probably) THE LYCEUM.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Son of Clinias! you wonder, I suppose, that I, who was the earliest of your admirers, now, when all the rest have forsaken you, am the only one who still retains unalterably the same sentiments; and yet, that for so many years I have never spoken so much as a word to you, whilst the others were pressing through crowds of people to converse with you. This reserve and distance in my behaviour have been owing to no human regards, but to an impediment thrown in my way by a dæmoniacal nature, the power and force of which you shall by and by be made acquainted with. But now, seeing that this power no longer

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: operates to hinder my approach, I am come thus to accost you; and am in good hopes too, that for the future the dæmon will give no opposition to my desire of conversing with you. All this while, however, being but a spectator, I have been able tolerably well to observe and consider your behaviour with regard to your admirers. And I find, that, though they have been numerous, and such persons too as thought highly of themselves, there is not one whom you have not driven away from you by your superior haughtiness and imagined elevation.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: The reasons of your being exalted so highly in your own opinion, I am desirous of laying before you. They are these: You presume, that in no affair whatever you need assistance from any other party: for that what you have of your own, whether of outward advantages or inward accomplishments, is so great as to be all-sufficient. In the first place, you think yourself excelling in the handsomeness of your person and in the fineness of your figure. And in this opinion it is evident to every one who has eyes that you are not mistaken. In the next place, you dwell on these thoughts: that you are descended from families the most illustrious in the state to which you belong; that this state is the greatest of any in Greece;

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: that you have friends here, and relations on your father’s side, very numerous and very powerful, ready to assist you on every occasion; and that your relations on your mother’s side are not inferior to them, either in power or in number. But a greater strength than from all these whom I have mentioned, taken together, you think that you derive from Pericles, the son of Xanthippus, whom your father left guardian to yourself and to your brother: Pericles, who is able to do what he pleases; and that, not only at Athens, but throughout all Greece, and with many and great families abroad.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: To all these advantages I shall add the greatness of your estate; though, indeed, on this advantage you seem to value yourself less than you do on any other. Elevated as you are in your own mind on these accounts, you have looked down on your admirers: and they, conscious of their comparative meanness, have bowed their heads, and have retired. This you are very sensible of: and therefore I well know that you wonder what I can have in my thoughts, or what hopes I can entertain, seeing that I quit you not, but continue my attachment to you still, when your other admirers have all forsaken you.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: This however, Socrates, perhaps you do not know, that

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: you have been a little beforehand with me. For I really had it in my mind to address you first, and to ask you these very questions: What can possibly be your meaning, and with what views or expectations is it, that you continually press on me, and, wherever I am, are assiduous to be there yourself? for I do in truth wonder, what your business can be with me, and should be very glad to be informed.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: You will hear me then, ’tis to be supposed, with willingness and attention, if you really are desirous, as you say you are, of knowing what I have in my thoughts. I speak therefore as to a person disposed to hear, and to stay till he has heard all.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: I am entirely so disposed: it is your part to speak.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: But observe this: you must not wonder, if, as I found it difficult to make a beginning, I should find it no less difficult to make an end.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: My good man, say all you have to say; for I shall not fail to attend to you.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: I must say it then: and though it is a hard task for any man to address the person whom he loves or admires, if that person be superior to flattery, yet I must adventure boldly to speak my mind. If, Alcibiades, I had observed you satisfied with those advantages of yours, which I just now enumerated; if you had appeared to indulge the fancy of spending your whole life in the enjoyment of them; I persuade myself, that my love and admiration of you would have long since left me.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: But that you entertain thoughts very different from such as those, I shall now show, and shall lay your own mind open before yourself. By these means you will also plainly perceive, how constantly and closely my mind has attended to you. My opinion of you then is this: That, if any of the gods were to put this question to you,—“Alcibiades!” were he to say, “whether do you choose to live in the possession of all the things which are at present yours; or do you prefer immediate death, if you are not permitted ever to acquire things greater?” in this case, it appears to me that you would make death your option. But what kind of expectations you live in, I shall now declare. You think, that, if you speedily make your appearance before the Athenian people in assembly, (and this

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: you purpose to do within a few days,) you shall be able to convince them, that you merit higher honours than were ever bestowed on Pericles, or any other person in any age: and having convinced them of this, you think that you will arrive at the chief power in the state; and if here at home, that you will then have the greatest weight and influence abroad; and not only so with the rest of the Grecian states, but with the barbarian nations too, as many as inhabit the same continent with us. And further: if the deity whom I before spoke of, allowing you larger limits, were to say to you, that “you must be contented with being the master here in Europe;

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: for that ’twill not be permitted you to pass over into Asia, nor to concern yourself with the administration of any affairs there;” it appears to me, that neither on these terms, thus limited, would you think life eligible; nor on any terms, indeed, that fell short of filling, in a manner, the whole world with your renown, and of being every where lord and master. I believe you deem no man that ever lived, excepting Cyrus and Xerxes, worth the speaking of. In fine, that you entertain such hopes as I have mentioned, I know with certainty, and speak not from mere conjecture. Now you, perhaps, conscious of the truth of what I have spoken, might say,

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: “What is all this to the account you promised to give me, of the reasons for which your attachment to me still continues?” I will tell you then, dear son of Clinias and Dinomache! That all these thoughts of yours should ever come to an end, is impossible without my help,—so great power I think myself to have with regard to your affairs and to yourself too. For this reason, I have long been of opinion, that the god did not as yet permit me to hold any conversation with you; and I waited for the time when he would give me leave. For, as

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: you entertain hopes of proving to the people, that your value to them is equal to whatever they can give you; and as you expect that, having proved this point, you shall immediately obtain whatever power you desire; in the same manner do I expect to have the greatest power and influence over you, when I shall have proved that I am valuable to you more than any other thing is; and that neither guardian, nor relation, nor any other person, is able to procure you the power you long for, except myself; with the assistance, however, of the god. So long therefore as you were yet too young, and before you had your mind filled with those swelling hopes, I believe that the god would not permit me to have discourse with you, because you would not have regarded me, and I consequently should have discoursed in vain; but that he has now given me free leave,

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: for that you would now hearken to me.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Much more unaccountable and absurd do you appear to me now, Socrates, since you have begun to open yourself, than when you followed me every where without speaking to me a word: and yet you had all the appearance of being a man of that sort then. As to what you have said, whether I entertain those thoughts in my mind, or not, you, it seems, know with certainty: so that, were I to say I did not, the denial would not avail me, nor persuade you to believe me. Admitting it then, and supposing that I indulge the hopes you mentioned ever so much, how they may be accomplished by means of you, and that without your help they never can, are you able to prove to me?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Do you ask me, whether I am able to prove it to you in a long harangue, such a one as you are accustomed to hear? I have no abilities in that way. But yet I should be able, as I think, to prove to you, that those pretensions of mine are not vain, if you would be willing but to do me one small piece of service.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: If that service be not difficult to be done, I am willing.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Do you think it difficult, or not, to make answers to such questions as are proposed to you?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Not difficult.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Be ready then to answer.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Do you then propose your questions.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: May I propose them, with a supposition that you have those thoughts in your mind

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: which I attribute to you?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Be it so, if you choose it; that I may know what further you have to say.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Well then. You have it in your mind, as I said, to appear in presence of the Athenians within a short time, with intention to harangue them and give them your advice. If therefore, when you are just ready to mount the rostrum, I were to stop you, and to say thus, “Since the Athenians are here met in assembly, on purpose to deliberate on some of their affairs, what, I pray you, are to be the subjects of their deliberation, now that you rise up to give them your counsel? Must not the subjects be such as you are better acquainted with than they?” what answer would you make me?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: I certainly should answer, that the subjects were such as I knew better than others who were present.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: On those subjects, then, which you happen to have knowledge in you are a good counsellor?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Without doubt.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Have you knowledge in those things only which you have either learnt from others, or found out yourself?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: What things other than those is it possible that I should have any knowledge in?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And is it possible that ever you should have learnt, or have found out, any thing which you were not willing to learn, or to search out by yourself?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: It is not.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And were you ever at any time willing to learn, or did you ever at any time seek to know, any things in which you imagined yourself to be already knowing?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: No, certainly.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: In those things which you now happen to know, was there once a time when you did not think yourself knowing?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: That must have been.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Now, what the things are which you have learnt, I tolerably well know. But if you have been taught any thing without my knowledge, tell me what. To the best of my memory, you have been taught grammar, the gymnic exercises, and to play on stringed instruments of music: for on wind-instruments, besides, you refused to learn. This is the sum total of all your knowledge; unless you have learnt any thing else in some place or other, which I have not discovered: and I think, that neither by day nor yet by night did you ever stir out of doors but I was acquainted with all your motions.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: ’Tis true that I have not gone to any other masters than to such as taught the arts which you have mentioned.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Well then. When the Athenians are consulting together about the grammar of their language, how to write or speak it with propriety, at these times is it that you will rise up to give them your advice?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: By Jove, not I.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: But is it then when they are in debate about striking chords on the lyre?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: By no means should I make a speech on such a subject.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: It cannot be on the subject of wrestling neither: because they never use to deliberate on this subject in their public assemblies.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Certainly not.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: On what subject, then, of their consultations is it that you intend the giving them your advice? It cannot be when building is the subject.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: No, certainly.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Because in this case a builder would give them better advice than you could.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: True.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Nor yet is it when they consult together concerning divination.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: It is not.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: For a diviner would in this case be a better counsellor than you.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Without doubt.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And that, whether he was a tall or a short man; whether his person was handsome or deformed; and whether his family was noble or ignoble.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: How should it be otherwise?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: For to give good advice in any case whatever, belongs, I suppose, only to a person skilled in the subject, and not to a fine gentleman.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Beyond all question.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And whether the man who gives them his advice be rich or poor, it will make no difference to the Athenians, when they are consulting

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: about the health of the city; but they will always inquire after a physician only to consult with.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: They will be right in so doing.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Now, on what subject is it, when they are met in consultation together, that you will do right in rising up and giving them your counsel?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: ’Tis when they are in consultation, Socrates, about their own affairs.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: About increasing their navy, do you mean? what sort of vessels they should provide, and in what manner they should have them built?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: I meant no such thing, Socrates.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Because you are ignorant, I presume, in the art of shipbuilding. Is not this the reason? Or is there any other, why you would choose in such a consultation to sit silent?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: That is the only reason.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: What affairs of their own then do you mean?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: I mean, Socrates, when they are deliberatii1g about the making war, or the making peace; or concerning any other affairs of state.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Do you mean, when they are deliberating on these points, with whom ’tis proper for them to make peace, and with whom to engage in war, and in what way ’tis proper to carry on that war? Is this what you mean?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: It is.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And you will agree, that ’tis proper to make peace or war with those people with whom ’tis best so to do?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Certainly.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And at that time when ’tis best?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: By all means.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And to continue it so long as ’tis best to continue it?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: To be sure.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Now, suppose that the Athenians were deliberating about the exercise of wrestling, with what sort of persons it is proper to come to close quarters, and with whom to engage at arm’s length, and in what way, would you give the best counsel in this case, or would a master of the exercises?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Such a master, certainly.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Can you tell me now, what end such a master would have in his view, when he gave his counsel on these points, with whom it is proper to wrestle closely, and with whom not so? at what times it is proper, and in what manner? My meaning is to ask you these questions: Whether is it proper to wrestle closely with those persons with whom it is best so to wrestle, or is it not?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: It is.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Whether as much also as is best?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: As much.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Whether at those times too when ’tis best?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Without doubt.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: But further: Ought not a singer sometimes, in singing, to touch his lute, and to move his feet?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: He ought.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Ought he not to do so at those times when ’tis best so to do?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Certainly.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And to continue the doing so as long as ’tis best to continue it?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: I agree.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Well now. Since you agree with me that there is a best in both these actions,

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: in fingering the lute whilst singing, and in the exercise of close wrestling, by what name call you that which is the best in fingering the lute? As that which is the best in wrestling I call gymnastical, what name now do you give to that which is best done in that other action?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: I do not apprehend your meaning.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Try to copy after the pattern which I shall now give you. Supposing, then, that I had been asked this question, “In wrestling, how is that performed which is performed best?” I should answer, ’Tis performed in every respect rightly. Now, in wrestling, that performance is right which is according to the rules of art. Is it not?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: It is.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And the art, in this case, is it not gymnastic?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Without dispute.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: I said, that that which is the best in wrestling is gymnastical.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: You did.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And was it not well said?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: I think it was.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Come then. Do you in like manner (for it would not ill become you likewise to discourse well) say, in the first place, What is the art, to which belong the playing on the harp, the singing, and the moving at the same time, rightly all; the whole of this art, by what name is it called? Are you not yet able to tell?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Indeed I am not.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Try in this way then. What goddesses are those who preside over this art?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: The muses mean you, Socrates?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: I do. Consider now, what name is given to their art—a name derived from them.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: I suppose you mean music.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: The very thing. What then is that which is performed rightly, according to this art? just as in the other case I told you, that whatever was performed rightly according to the rules of that other art, was gymnastical; in this case now, after the same manner, whatever is performed agreeably to the rules of this art; how do you say it must be performed?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Musically, I think.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: You say well. Let us now proceed further; and tell me, what name you give to that which is best in making war; and what name to that which is best in making peace:

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: just as, in the former cases, the best in one of them you called the more musical, in the other the more gymnastical. Try now in these cases likewise to name that which is the best.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: I find myself quite unable to tell what it is.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: ’Tis a shame to you that you are so. For, suppose you were speaking and giving your opinion concerning the superiority of one kind of food to another, and should say, that such or such a kind of food was the best at this season, and such or such a quantity of it; and suppose a man should thereupon question you thus, “What do you mean by the best, Alcibiades?” on these subjects you would be able to give him an answer, and to tell him, that by the best you meant the most wholesome; and this you would say, notwithstanding that you do not profess to be a physician. And yet, on a subject which you

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: profess to have the knowledge of, and rise up to give your judgment and advice on, as if you had this knowledge, are you not ashamed, when you are questioned, as I think you are, on this very subject, to be unable to give an answer, and to tell what is that which is the best? And must not this inability appear to others shameful in you?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Certainly it must.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Consider thoughtfully now, and tell me, What is the end or aim of that which is done best in the making or the continuing of peace, and likewise in the going to war with those with whom it is proper?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Well, I do consider; but cannot think of what it is.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Know you not, when we go to war, what it is which both the parties accuse each other of during their military preparations,

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: and what names they give to the causes of their quarrels?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: I do. They accuse each other of deceiving, or of offering violence, or of taking away some of their possessions.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: But observe: How do they say they have been thus treated? Try to tell me what difference there is in the manner of this treatment they give to each other.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Do you mean, whether they thus treat each other justly or unjustly?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: This is the very difference I mean.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: These different manners of ill treatment differ totally and entirely.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Well then. With whom would you counsel the Athenians to engage in war? whether with those who treat them ill unjustly, or with those who treat them as they deserve?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: A question, this, of very serious import. For, if any man should entertain a thought of the propriety of going to war with such as act uprightly, he would not dare to own it.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Because it is not lawful, I suppose, to engage in such a war.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: By no means is it so, neither seems it to be beautiful.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: With a view therefore to these things, and to what is just, you will make your speeches to the people.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: There is a necessity for bringing my arguments from these topics.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: That best then, concerning which I just now asked you what it was,—the best on these subjects,—whether it is proper to go to war or not, with whom it is proper, and with whom not,—at what times it is proper, and when not,—does the best on these subjects appear to be any other thing than that which is the most agreeable to justice? or does it not?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: It appears to be no other thing.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: How is this, friend Alcibiades? Is it a secret to yourself, that you are ignorant in the science of justice? or else, Is it a secret to me, that you have learnt it, and have gone to some master, who has taught you to distinguish between what is the most agreeable to justice, and what is the most repugnant to it? If this which I last mentioned be the case, who is this master? Tell me; that I too may go and learn of him, through your recommendation.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: You banter, Socrates.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Not so; by the guardian-god of friendship to both of us, you and me, whose deity

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: I would least of all invoke for witness to a falsehood! If then you have any master who teaches you that science, let me know who he is.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: And what if I have not? Do you think that I could by no other means have attained the knowledge of what is just, and what is unjust?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: I think that you would, if you had discovered it by yourself.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Are you then of opinion that I could not have discovered it by myself?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: I am entirely of opinion that you might, if ever you had sought for it.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Do you presume, then, that I have never sought for it?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: I should presume that you had, if ever you had thought yourself ignorant of it.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Was there not then a time when I so thought?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Well said. Can you tell me, then, at what time

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: you did not imagine yourself to know what things are just, and what are unjust? For, come, let me ask you: Was it last year, when you inquired into these subjects, and did not imagine yourself already knowing in them? or did you at that time think that you had such knowledge? Answer truly now, that our argument may come to some conclusion.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Well then. I did at that time presume myself to be knowing in those subjects.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And in all the third year back from this present, in all the fourth too, and all the fifth, did you not presume of yourself the same?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: I did.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And earlier than the time I mentioned last, you were but a boy.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: True.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And in your days of boyhood I am well assured that you thought yourself knowing in those subjects.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: How are you so sure of that?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Often in the schools, when you were a boy, and in other places too whenever you were playing at dice, or were a party in any other play, I have heard you talking about what things were just or unjust—not as if you had any doubts on those subjects, but very strenuously and boldly pronouncing, that such or such a one of your play-mates was a wicked boy, and a rogue, and was guilty of a piece of injustice. Is not all this true?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Well. But what else was I to do, when any of them injured me?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Right. But if you had happened to be ignorant of this very point, whether you were injured or not, would you say, “What in such a case was I to do?”

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: But, by Jove, I was not ignorant of that point; for I clearly saw that I was injured.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: You thought yourself, it seems, therefore, when you were a boy, knowing in the science of what is just and what is unjust?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: I did so; and knowing in it I was too.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: At what time was it that you first discovered it? for certainly it was not at a time when you thought yourself knowing in it.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: That, ’tis clear, could not be.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: At what time then was it that you thought yourself ignorant in it? Consider: but that time you will never find.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: By Jove, Socrates, I am not able to tell when.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: You did not acquire that knowledge, then, by any discovery of your own?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: That does not at all appear to have been the case.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And besides, you acknowledged but just before, that you did not acquire it by being taught. If then you neither discovered it of yourself, nor were taught it by any other person, how or whence have you this knowledge?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Well. But I was wrong in my answers, when I supposed that I had found out that knowledge by myself.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: In what way then did you acquire it?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: I learnt it, I presume, in the same way in which others do.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: We are now come round again to the same question as before: From whom did you learn it? Inform me.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: From the people.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: To no good teachers have you recourse for the origin of your knowledge, in referring it to the people.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Why so? Are not they capable of teaching?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Not so much as what movements are proper, and what improper, to make in a game at tables. And yet the knowledge of these things is meaner and more inconsiderable, in my opinion, than the knowledge of what things are just and what are unjust. Do not you think so too?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: I do.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Incapable, therefore, as they are of teaching meaner things, can they teach things higher and of more importance?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: I think they can. Nay, it is certain that they are capable of teaching many things of more importance than the movements in a game at tables.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: What things do you mean?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Such as, for instance, to speak the Greek language: for I myself learnt it from them. Nor could I name any other teacher of that language that I ever had; but must refer my being able to speak it to those very persons who you say are no good teachers.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Well, my noble sir: in this matter, indeed, the people are good teachers,, and as such may justly be recommended.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Why particularly in this?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Because in this they possess all the requisites necessary to every good teacher.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: What requisites do you mean?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Do you not know, that those who are to teach any thing must in the first place have the knowledge of it themselves? Must they not?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Without doubt.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And must not all those who have the knowledge of any thing agree together on that subject, and not differ in their opinions of it?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Certainly.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: But where they differ among themselves in their opinions, would you say that they have, all of them, knowledge in those subjects?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Certainly not.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Of such things, then, how can they be good teachers?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: By no means can they.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Well now. Do the people seem to you to differ among themselves about the meaning of the words stone and wood? Ask whom you will,

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: are they not all agreed in the same opinion? And when they are bid to take up a stone, or a piece of wood, do they not all go to the same kind of things? And do they not all apprehend alike, what kind of things every other such word signifies? For I presume this is what you mean by knowledge of the Greek language: is it not?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: It is.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Now, on these subjects, as we said before, do not the people of our city agree among themselves? And among the several cities of Greece is there any difference of opinion? Do the same words, in different places signify different things?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: They do not.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: On these subjects, therefore, agreeably to our argument, the people should be good teachers.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: It is true.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: If then we had a mind to have any person instructed in this matter, we should do right in sending him, for such instruction amongst the multitude of the people?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Quite right.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: But what if we had a mind to have that person taught, not only to know men from horses by the different words denoting them in the Greek language, but, beside this, to know what horses are fit for the race, and what are unfit? is the multitude able to teach this also?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Certainly not.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And you admit this to be a sufficient proof of their ignorance in this matter,

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: and of their inability to teach, that they agree not in their opinions on this head?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: I do.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And what if we would have him learn, not only by what word in our language men are distinguished from other things, but, further, to know what men are healthy and who are unhealthy? whether should we deem the multitude to be the proper teachers for him?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: By no means.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And it would be an evidence to you of their being bad teachers on this subject, if you saw them disagreeing in their opinions?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: It would.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And how is it now on the subject of justice? Do you find the multitude agreeing one with another,

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: or even the same person always of the same mind, concerning either men or actions, who are the honest, or what is just?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Less than on any other subject, by Jove, Socrates, are they agreed with regard to this.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: What? do you then think they differ on this subject more than upon any other?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: By far do they.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: You have never, I suppose, seen or heard of men, in any age, who contended for their several opinions concerning the wholesome and the unwholesome in food, with so much zeal as to fight and kill one another on that account?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Never.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: But concerning just and unjust in actions, that their disputes have carried them to such extremities, I am sure,

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: if you have not seen, you have at least heard from many reports, and particularly from those of Homer; for you have heard both the Odyssey and the Iliad read to you.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Thoroughly well, Socrates, am I versed in both.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And is not the subject of both these poems the diversity of opinions with regard to what is just and what is unjust?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: It is.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And did not this diversity of opinions produce fighting and slaughter between the Greeks and Trojans, and between Ulysses and the wooers of Penelope?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: True.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And I believe that the deaths of those Athenians, Lacedæmonians and Bœotians, who perished at Tanagra, and of those who afterwards died at Coronea, amongst whom was Clinias your father, were not owing to differences on any other subject than this, what was just and what unjust.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: You are in the right.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Shall we say then that these people had knowledge in that subject on which

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: they differed with so much vehemence, as in support of their different opinions to suffer from each other the utmost effects of hatred?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: It appears they had not.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Do you not then refer to such a sort of teachers as you yourself acknowledge to be ignorant?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: I do, it seems.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: How therefore is it probable that you should have the knowledge to discern what is just from what is unjust, when your account of them is so vague, and when you appear neither to have been taught that knowledge by any other person, nor to have found it out yourself?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: According to what you say, ’tis not probable.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Are you sensible that what you said last was not said fairly, Alcibiades?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: What was unfair?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Your assertion that I said those things of you which were said.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: What? did not you say that I had not the knowledge to discern what was just from what was unjust?.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Not I, indeed.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Who was it then that said so? was it myself?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: It was.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Make that appear.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: You will see it in this way. If I ask you concerning one and two, which is the greater number, you will say that two is.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: I shall.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: How much greater is it?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Greater by one.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Now whether of us is it who says that two is a greater number or more than one by one?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: It is I myself.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Did not I ask the question, and did not you give an answer to it?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: True: it was so.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: On this subject, then, who appears to have made any assertion? Do I, who only asked a question? or do you, who gave the answer?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: I.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And if I ask you how many letters compose the name of Socrates, and you tell me, which of us is it who declares how many?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: I.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: In a word, whenever any question is asked, and an answer to it is given, say, who is it that makes an assertion, the party that asks the question, or the party that gives the answer?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: The party that gives the answer, in my opinion, Socrates.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Through the whole of our past discourse was not I the party that asked the questions?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: You were.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And were not you the party that gave the answers?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: I was.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Well then. Whether of us two made the assertions?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: From what I have admitted, Socrates, I myself appear to have been that person.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: In those assertions was it not said that Alcibiades, the fine son of Clinias, had not the knowledge to discern what was just and what was unjust, but imagined that he had; and that he was about going into the assembly to give the Athenians his counsel and advice upon subjects which he knew nothing of? Is not this true?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: It appears so to be.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: That which Euripides says may therefore well be applied to the condition you are now in, Alcibiades. You are in danger of being found to have heard all this which has been said of you from yourself, and not from me. For, not I, but you, was the assertor of it; and you lay the blame of it on me without reason.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Indeed, Socrates, you are in the right.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Mad therefore is the undertaking, my good sir, which you entertain thoughts of attempting, to teach others what you are ignorant of yourself from your having neglected to learn it.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: I believe, Socrates, that the Athenians, as well as other Grecian states, seldom deliberate in council about justice or injustice in any affair before them; because these things they presume obvious and plain to all men. Laying aside therefore the consideration of this point, they consider which way it will be most for their interest to take. For I suppose that justice and interest are not the same thing; seeing that many have found it their interest to have done things the most unjust, and that others have gained no advantage from having acted with honesty.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Well. Suppose interest to be a thing ever so different from justice,

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: do you imagine now that you know what is a man’s interest, and why this or that thing is so?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: What should hinder me, Socrates, from knowing it? Unless you will make a doubt of this too, by asking me, from whom I learned this knowledge, or how I discovered it myself.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: How strangely you deal with me in this? If you say any thing wrong, when ’tis possible to prove it wrong by the same arguments used in confuting what you before said amiss, you would have new matter introduced, and different arguments made use of, to prove you in the wrong again: as if the former proofs were worn out like old clothes, and you could no longer put them on, but one must bring you a fresh proof never used before.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: But without taking further notice of your evasions, I shall repeat the same question, and ask you from what learning you came to know what was a man’s interest, and who taught you this knowledge; and all the other questions asked before I ask you again, summing them up in one. It is evident now, that your answers will amount to the very same as they did before; and that you will not be able to show by what means you attained the knowledge of what is advantageous to a man; or conducive to his good; either how you found it out yourself, or from whom you learned it. However, seeing that you are squeamish, and decline the tasting of the same arguments again, I wave the inquiry into this point, whether you have or not the knowledge

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: of what is the interest of the Athenians. But this other point, whether the same actions are just and advantageous; or whether what ’tis just to do, differs from what ’tis a man’s interest to do; why should not you prove, by putting questions to me, in the same manner as I did to you? or, if you had rather, make a discourse upon that subject wholly by yourself.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: But I know not if I should be able, Socrates, to make such a discourse to you.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Why, my good friend, suppose me to be the assembly and the people. And, were you addressing your discourse to them, it would be proper for you to persuade every single man of them. Would it not?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: It would.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Does it not belong, then, to the same person to be able to persuade one single man by himself

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: and to persuade many men assembled together, in speaking on any subject with which he is well acquainted? as, for instance, a teacher of grammar is equally well able to persuade one man and many men, when letters are the subject of his discourse.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: True.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And when numbers are the subject, would not the same person who persuades many, persuade one as well?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: He would.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And must not this person be one who is well acquainted with numbers must he not be an arithmetician?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Most certainly.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And would not you also, in speaking on any subjects, if you are able to persuade many of the truth of what you say, be able to persuade a single one?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: ’Tis probable that I should.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: But these subjects it is plain must be such as you are well acquainted with.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Undoubtedly.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Is there any other difference, then, between a speaker

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: in the assembly of the people and a speaker in such conversation as this of ours, than merely so much as this—the former endeavours to persuade a collection of many men—the latter to persuade men one by one?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: There appears to be no other.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Come then. Since it apparently belongs to the same person to persuade a multitude and to persuade a single man, practice your skill on me, and undertake to prove to me that in some cases that which is just is not a man’s interest.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: You are very saucy, Socrates.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And I am now going to be so saucy as to convince you of the truth of a position quite contrary to that which you decline the proving of to me.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Begin then.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Do you but answer to the questions which I shall put to you.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Not so: but do you yourself say plainly what you have to say.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Why so? Would you not choose to be entirely well persuaded of the truth of it, if it be true?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: By all means, certainly.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And would you not, if you yourself were to assert it, have the most entire persuasion of its truth?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: I think so.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Answer then to my questions: and if you do not hear from your own mouth, that to act justly is to act for one’s own advantage, believe no other person who asserts that position.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: I shall not: and I consent to answer your questions. For no harm I think will come to me that way.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: You think as if you had the spirit of divination. Tell me, then: Do you say that some just actions are advantageous to the man who performs them, and that some are not so?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: I do.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And do you say also, that some just actions are beautiful, and that some are not so?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: What mean you by this question?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Whether did you ever think that a man acted basely and yet justly at the same time?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: I never thought so.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: You think then that all actions which are just are also beautiful?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: I do.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: But what, as to actions which are beautiful? Whether do you think that all of these are good to the performer, or that some of them are so, and some not so?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: For my part, Socrates, I think that some beautiful actions are evil to the performer of them.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And that some base actions are good to the performer?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: I do.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Do you mean such actions as these?—Many men by aiding in battle some friend or near relation have been wounded mortally; whilst others, by withholding their aid when they ought to have given it, have come off safe and sound.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: A just instance of what I mean.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: That aid then of theirs you call beautiful with respect to their endeavouring to save those whom they ought to defend. Now such an action proceeds from fortitude, does it not?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: It does.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: But evil you call it also with respect to the wounds and death which it procured them, do you not?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: I do.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And are not fortitude and death two different things?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Certainly.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: To aid a friend, therefore, is not both beautiful and evil in the same respect?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: It appears that ’tis not.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Consider now whether it be not good in the same respect in which it is beautiful; as in this particular which we mentioned. For, with respect to fortitude, you agreed with me that ’twas beautiful and handsome to give such aid. This very thing then, fortitude, consider whether it be a good or an evil. And consider it in this way:—which kind of things would you choose to have your own, whether good things or evil things?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Good things.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And would you not choose the best things too?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Most of all things.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And would you not choose to part with them least of all?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Undoubtedly.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: What say you then of fortitude? at what price would you choose to part with it?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: I would not accept of life, not I, to live a coward.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: You think, then, that cowardice is evil in the utmost degree?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: That do I.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: On a par, as it seems, with death.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: It is so.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Are not life and fortitude the most of all things opposite to death and cowardice?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: They are.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And would you choose to have those most of all things, and these least of all things?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Certainly.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Is it because you deem those the best of all things, and these the worst?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: For this very reason.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Viewing then the giving of aid in battle to such as are dear to us in that light in which it appears beautiful—viewing it with regard to the practice of that virtue which you acknowledge to be one of the best of things, you gave it the epithet of beautiful?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: It appears I did so.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: But with regard to its operating evil, the evil of death, you gave it the epithet of evil?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: True.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Is it not then just and right to denominate every action thus? If, with regard to the evil which it operates, you call it evil, ought it not,

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: with regard to the good which it operates, to be also called good?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: I think it ought.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: In the same respect, then, in which it is good, is it not beautiful? and in the same respect in which it is evil, is it not base?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: It is.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: In saying, then, that the aiding of our friends in battle is an action beautiful indeed, but that yet ’tis evil, you say exactly the same thing as if you called it an action, good indeed, but yet evil.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: I think you are in the right, Socrates.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Nothing therefore which is beautiful, so far as it is beautiful, is evil; nor is any thing which is base, so far as it is base, good.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Evidently it is not.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Further now consider it in this way:—whoever acts beautifully, does he not act well too?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: He does.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And those who act well, are they not happy?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Without doubt.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And are they not happy by being possessed of good things?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Most certainly.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And are they not possessed of these good things by acting well and beautifully?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: They are.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: To act well, therefore, is in the rank of good things?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Beyond a doubt.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And is not acting well a beautiful thing also?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: It is.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Again therefore we have found, that one and the same thing is both beautiful and good?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: We have.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Whatever then we should find to be a beautiful thing, we shall find it to be a good thing too, according to this reasoning?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: It must be so.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And what? are good things advantageous? or are they not?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: They are.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Do you remember, now, what we agreed in concerning things which are just?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: I imagine that you mean this,—that those persons who do things which are just must of necessity do things which at the same time are beautiful.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And did we not agree in this too,—that those who do things which are beautiful do things which are also good?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: We did.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And good things, you say, are advantageous?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: True.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Things therefore which are just, O Alcibiades! are things which are advantageous.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: It seems they are.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Well now; are not you the person who asserts these things? and am not I the questioner concerning them?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: So it appears.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Whoever then rises up to speak in any council, whether it be of Athenians or Peparethians, imagining that he discerns what is just and what is unjust, if he should say that he knows justice to be sometimes evil and detrimental, would you not laugh at his pretensions to knowledge? since you yourself are found to be the very person who asserts that

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: the same things are both just and advantageous?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Now, by the Gods, Socrates, for my part, I know not what to say to it; but am quite like a man distracted. For sometimes I am of one opinion, just while you are putting your questions to me, and presently after am of another.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Are you ignorant now, my friend, what condition you are in?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Entirely ignorant.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Do you imagine, then, that if any person were to ask you, how many eyes you had, whether two or three,—or how many hands, whether two or four,—or any other such question,—you would sometimes answer one thing, and at other times another? or would you always give the same answer?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: I confess that I am now doubtful of myself; but I do believe that I should always give the same answer.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
