segments.text: SOCRATES: And is not your knowledge of the subject the cause of that consistency there would be in your answers?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: I believe it is.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: When therefore you give contrary answers to one and the same question, without choosing to prevaricate, ’tis evident that you have no knowledge of the subject.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Probably so.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Now you say that, to questions concerning things just or unjust, beautiful or base, good or evil, advantageous or otherwise, you should answer sometimes one thing and sometimes another. Is it not then evident, that your ignorance in these subjects is the cause of this inconsistency of yours?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: It appears so to me myself.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Is not this then the true state of the case? On every subject which a man has not the knowledge of, must not his soul be wavering in her opinions?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Most undoubtedly.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Well now. Do you know by what means you may mount up to heaven?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: By Jupiter, not I.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Is your opinion doubtful and wavering on this subject?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Not at all.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Do you know the reason why it is not? or shall I tell it you?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Do you tell me.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: ’Tis this, my friend: it is because you neither know nor imagine that you know the way up to heaven.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: How is that the reason? Explain yourself.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Let you and I consider it together. Concerning any affairs which you are ignorant of, and are at the same time convinced that you are so, do you waver in your opinions? For instance, in the affair of dressing meats and making sauces, you are, I presume, well acquainted with your ignorance.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Perfectly well.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Do you form any opinions then yourself on these affairs of cookery, and waver in those opinions? or do you leave those matters to such as are skilled in them?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: I do as you mentioned last.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And what if you were in a ship under sail, would you form any opinion,

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: whether the rudder ought to be turned toward the ship or from it, and be unsettled in that opinion for want of knowledge in the affair? or would you leave it to the pilot, and not trouble yourself about it?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: To the pilot I should leave it.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Concerning affairs then which you are ignorant of, and are no stranger to your own ignorance in those respects, you are not wavering in your opinions?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: I believe I am not.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Do you perceive that errors, committed in the doing of any thing, are all to be ascribed to this kind of ignorance in a man,—his imagining that he knows what he knows not?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: How do you mean?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Whenever we undertake to act in any affair, it is only when we imagine we know what to do.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Certainly.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And such as have no opinion of their own knowledge in the affair resign it up to others to act for them.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: How should they do otherwise?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Ignorant persons of this kind live therefore without committing errors, because they give up the management of those affairs in which they are ignorant into the hands of others.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: True.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: What kind of persons, then, are those who err and act amiss? For certainly they are not such as know how to act.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: By no means.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Since then they are neither the knowing, nor those of the ignorant

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: who know that they are ignorant, are any other persons left than of that kind who are ignorant, but imagine themselves knowing?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: None other than these.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: This kind of ignorance, therefore, is the cause of wrong doings, and is the only kind which is culpable.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Very true.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And where it concerns things of greatest moment, is it not in these cases the most of any mischievous and shameful?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: By far the most so.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Well then. Can you name any things of greater moment than those which are honest, and beautiful, and good, and advantageous?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Certainly none.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Is it not on these subjects that you acknowledge yourself to waver in your opinions?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: It is.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And, if you are thus wavering, is it not evident from our past conclusions,

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: not only that you are ignorant in subjects of the greatest moment, but that amidst this ignorance you imagine that you know them?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: I fear it is so.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Fie upon it, Alcibiades! What a condition then are you in! a condition which I am loth to name: but however, since we are alone, it must be spoken out. You are involved, my good sir, in that kind of ignorance which is the most shameful, according to the result of our joint reasoning, and according to your own confession. From this kind of ignorance it is, that you are eager to engage in politics before you have learnt the elements of that science. Indeed, you are not the only person in this sad condition; for in the same state of ignorance are the numerous managers of our civil affairs,

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: all of them, except perhaps Pericles, your guardian, and a few more.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: And, Socrates, to confirm this opinion of yours, Pericles is said to have become wise, not spontaneously or of himself: on the contrary, ’tis reported of him that he had had the advantage of enjoying the conversation of many wise men, particularly of Pythoclides a11d Anaxagoras: and even at this time, old as he is, he is intimate with Damon for this very purpose.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: But what? have you ever seen a man who was wise in any art whatever, and yet was unable to make another man wise in the same art? as, for instance, the master who taught you grammar was himself wise in that art; and in the same art he made you wise; as he also made every other person whom he undertook to teach. Did he not?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: He did.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And you, who have learnt from him that kind of wisdom, would not you be able to teach it to another person?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Certainly I should.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And is not the same thing true of a music-master and of a master in the exercises?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Perfectly so.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: For this undoubtedly is a fair proof of the knowledge of such as are knowing in any subject whatever, their being able to produce their scholars, and to show these to be knowing in the same.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: I think so too.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Well then. Can you name to me any one whom Pericles has made a wise man? his own sons has he? to begin with them.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: But what if the sons of Pericles were silly fellows, Socrates?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Clinias then, your brother?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Why should you mention Clinias, a man out of his senses?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Since Clinias then is out of his senses, and since the sons of Pericles were silly fellows, to what defect in your disposition shall we impute the little care taken by Pericles to improve you?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: I presume that I myself am in the fault that of not giving due attention to him.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: But name any person else, an Athenian or a foreigner, either a slave or a free man, who is indebted to the instructions of Pericles for becoming wiser than he was: as I can name to you those, who from the lessons of Zeno have improved in wisdom,—Pythodorus the son of Isolochus, and Callias the son of Calliades; each of whom, at the price of a hundred minæ, paid to Zeno, became eminent for wisdom.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Now, by Jupiter, I cannot.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Very well. What then do you think of doing about yourself whether to rest satisfied in the condition which you are now in, or to apply yourself to some means of improvement?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Concerning this, Socrates, I would consult with you. For I apprehend what you have said, and admit the truth of it. Those who have the administration of the state, except a few of them, seem indeed to me too, not to have had a proper education.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Well; and what conclusion do you draw from thence?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: This,—that if they, through their education, were well qualified to govern, a man who should undertake to enter the lists in contest with them, ought to come to the engagement duly prepared by discipline and exercise, as in other combats. But now, seeing that such persons as these, raw and undisciplined as they are, have attained to the management of state-affairs, what need is there for a man to exercise himself in such matters, or to give himself the trouble of acquiring knowledge in them?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: For I well know, that by dint of natural abilities I shall excel them by far, and get above them.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Fie upon it, my fine young gentleman! What a declaration is this which you have made! how unworthy of your personal qualities, and of the other advantages you are possessed of!

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: I should be glad, Socrates, to know why you think it unworthy of me, and in what respect.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: You offer an affront, not only to the regard which I have for you, but to the opinion too which you have of yourself.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: How so?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: In that you think of entering the lists to contend with these men here at Athens.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Whom then am I to contend with?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Does this question become a man to ask who thinks his mind to be great and elevated?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: How do you mean? Is it not with these very persons that I am to stand in competition?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Let me ask you this question;—Whether, if you had any thoughts of commanding a ship of war, would you deem it sufficient for you to excel the mariners who were to be under your command, in the skill belonging to a commander? or, presuming yourself qualified with this due præ-excellence would you direct your eye to those only whom you are in fact to combat against,—and not, as you now do, to such as are in combat together with you? For to these men certainly you ought to be so much superior, that they should never be your associates in competition against any, but

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: your inferior assistants in combating against the enemy;—if you really think of exhibiting any noble exploits worthy of yourself and of your country.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: And such a thought I assure you that I entertain.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Is it then at all worthy of you, to be contented with being a better man than your fellow-soldiers,—and not to have your eye directed toward the leaders of those whom you have to struggle with, studying how to become a better man than they, and employing yourself in exercise which are proper with a view to them?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: What persons do you mean, Socrates?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Do you not know, that our city is every now and then at war with the Lacedæmonians, and with the Great King!

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: True.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: If then you have it in your mind to be the leader of this city, would you not think rightly in thinking that you will have the kings of Sparta and of Persia to contend against?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: I suspect that you are in the right.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And yet you, my good sir, on the contrary, are to fix your view on Midias,

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: a feeder of quails, and on other such persons, who undertake to manage affairs of state, still wearing the badge of slavery (as the women would term it) in their souls, through their ignorance of the Muses; and not having yet thrown it off, but retaining their old sentiments, and manners still barbarian, are come to flatter the people, not to govern them. Ought you now to emulate these men whom I am speaking of, and disregard yourself? Ought you to neglect the acquiring of all such knowledge, as only is acquired through learning, when you have so great a combat to sustain? Or ought you to omit the exercising yourself in all such actions as

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: are well performed only through practice? Should you not be furnished with all the qualifications requisite for the government of the state before you undertake to govern it?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Indeed, Socrates, I believe you are in the right: but however, I imagine the commanders of the Spartan armies, and the Persian monarch, to be just such men as the others whom you have mentioned.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: But, my very good sir, consider this imagination of yours, what evils attend on it.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: In what respects?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: In the first place, What opinion concerning your antagonists do you think would engage you to take most care about yourself?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: whether the opinion of their being formidable, or the contrary?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: The opinion without doubt of their being formidable.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And do you think it would do you any harm to take care about yourself?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: None at all; but on the contrary great good.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: The want of this great good, then, is one of the evils which attend on that imagination?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: It is true.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Consider if there be not probably another too; and that is the falsity of it.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: How do you prove that?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Whether is it probable that persons, the most excellent in their natural dispositions

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: are to be found amongst those who descend from ancestors the noblest? or is it not?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Undoubtedly it is.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And is it not probable that such as have excellent dispositions from nature, if they meet with a suitable education, should become accomplished an virtue?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Of necessity they must.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Let us consider now, in comparing their advantages with our own, whether the kings of Sparta and of Persia seem to be descended from meaner ancestors than we are. Know we not that those are descendants of Hercules, and these of Achæmenes? that the begetting of Hercules is attributed to Jupiter, and the ancestry of Achæmenes to Perseus the son of Jupiter?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: And the family which I am of, o Socrates! descends from Eurysaces; and the descent of Eurysaces was from Jupiter.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And the family which I am of, my noble Alcibiades! descends from Dædalus; and the descent of Dædalus was from Vulcan, the son of Jupiter. But the pedigree of those with whom we set ourselves in comparison, beginning from the persons who now reign, exhibits a race of kings, all of them sons of kings, in a direct line quite up to Jupiter; those whom I first mentioned, kings of Argos and Lacedæmon; the others, kings of Persia perpetually, and often of all Asia, as they are at present: whereas we are but private men, ourselves and our fathers. If you then

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: were to boast of your ancestors, and pompously say that Salamis was the hereditary dominion of Eurysaces, or, to ascend higher in your ancestry, that Æacus governed in his native country Ægina, can you imagine how ridiculous you would appear in the eyes of Artaxerxes, the son of Xerxes? Consider besides, whether we may not be found inferior to those great men, not only in the pride of ancestry, but also in the care taken of our birth and breeding. Are you not sensible of the singular advantages which attend the progeny of the Spartan kings in this respect, that their wives have a guard of state appointed for them by the Ephori; to the end that no king of theirs may be the issue of stolen embraces,

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: or have for his real father any other man than a descendant of Hercules? And as to the Persian king, so greatly is he our superior with regard to this point, that none of his subjects entertain the least suspicion of his having any other father than the king his predecessor. The consort therefore of the king of Persia is under no restraint but that of her own dread of the evil consequences, should she dishonour the king’s bed. Further, when the king’s eldest son, the heir apparent to the crown, is born, all the king’s subjects in the city of his residence keep that day an original feast-day: and from thenceforward the anniversary of that day is celebrated with sacrifices and feasts by all Asia. But when we came first into the world, alas, Alcibiades! our very neighbours, as the comic poet says,

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: little knew what happened. After this the child is brought up, not by some insignificant nurse, but by the best eunuchs about the king’s person. And these have it in their charge to take care of the royal infant in every respect, but especially to contrive the means of his becoming as handsome as possible in his person, by so fashioning his pliant limbs, and giving such a direction to their growth, that they may be straight: and for executing this office well they are highly honoured.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: When the young princes have attained the age of seven years, they are provided with horses and with riding-masters, and are initiated in the exercise of hunting. At fourteen years of age they are put into the hands of those who are called the royal preceptors. And these are chosen out from such as are deemed the most excellent of the Persians, men of mature age, four in number; excelling severally in wisdom, justice, temperance,

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: and fortitude. By the first of these they are taught the magic of Zoroaster after the son of Oromazes [Ormazd], by which magic is meant the worship of the Gods: and the same person instructs them likewise in the art of government. He who excels in the science of justice teaches them to follow truth in every part of their conduct throughout life. The person who excels in temperance enures the young prince not to be governed by sensual pleasure of any kind, that he may acquire the habits of a free man, and of a real king; by governing first all his own appetites, instead of being their slave. And the fourth, he who excels in fortitude forms his royal pupil to be fearless and intrepid; for that his mind, under the power of fear, would be a slave. But,

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: Alcibiades, for your preceptor Pericles appointed one of his domestics, too old to be fit for any other service, Zopyrus of Thrace. I would recount to you the other articles of the breeding and instruction given to your antagonists, if the narration would not be too long; and besides this,, the articles already mentioned are sufficient indications of those others which they infer and draw along with them. But your birth, Alcibiades, your breeding and institution, or any other circumstances at tending you, scarce any one of the Athenians is at all solicitous about, unless there be some man who happens to have an especial regard for you. Further; if you would consider the treasures

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: of the Persian kings, the sumptuous furniture of their palaces and tables, their wardrobes of apparel, the long trains of their garments, and the fragrancy of their unguents, their numerous retinue of attendants, and the rest of their magnificence, in comparing all this with what you have of the same kind yourself, you would evidently perceive how much you fall short of them, and would be ashamed at the comparison. If, on the other hand, you would consider the Lacedæmonians, their sobriety and modesty, how simple their way of living, and how easily they are satisfied, their magnanimity and observance of order, their manly endurance of pain and love of labour, their emulation to excel, and their love of honour, you would think yourself a child

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: to them in all these excellencies. Besides this, if you make riches any part of your consideration, and in this respect imagine yourself a person of consequence, let us not pass over this point neither unexamined; if by any means you can be made sensible in what rank you stand. If you choose then to consider the Lacedæmonians with regard to wealth, you will find that what we have here in Attica falls far short of theirs. For the lands which they possess in their own country, and in Messenia, are such as that no person here would dispute their superiority in this respect, whether he considers the quantity or the value of those lands, the number of their other slaves, besides such as the Helotes, or the number of their horses,

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: and other cattle in the pasture-grounds of Messenia. But, setting aside all this, you will find that, as to gold and silver, there is not so much amongst all the Grecians as there is amongst the Lacedæmonians in private hands. For gold and silver have now for many generations been flowing into them from all parts of Greece, and often too from foreign countries; but there is no reflux any way. That therefore which the fox said to the lion in a fable of Æsop’s,

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: may justly be applied to them; the footsteps of money coming into Lacedæmon are easy to be discovered, as being all turned towards it; but the tracks of money going out of it are no where to be discerned. Thus it may easily be conceived, that of all the Grecians the richest in gold and silver are the Lacedæmonians, and that of all the Lacedæmonians the richest is their king. For of such comings-in a larger share, and oftener, is received by kings than by other men.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: And besides this, the taxes paid by the Lacedæmonians to their kings bring them in a large revenue. But whatever wealth the Lacedæmonians have, though great if compared with that of any other Grecians, yet in comparison with the riches of the Persians, and especially of their king, ’tis nothing. For I once heard a man of credit, who had been at the capital city of Persia, say, that in going up to it, he travelled almost a day’s journey through a large and fertile territory, which the inhabitants of it called the Queen’s Girdle; that there was another extensive tract of land called the Queen’s Veil;

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: and that many other fair and fruitful countries were appropriated to provide the rest of the queen’s apparel; each of those countries having its name from that part of the apparel which the revenue of it furnished. So that, were any person to tell the queen-mother, Amastris, the consort formerly of Xerxes, that the son of Dinomache had it in his head to lead an army against her son; and were she told at the same time that Dinomache’s whole attire might be worth perhaps fifty minæ; supposing it to be of the most costly kind; and that this son of hers had land in the district of Erchia, containing not so much as three hundred acres; she I suppose would wonder in what kind of things this

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: Alcibiades could place so much confidence as to think of contending with Artaxerxes. And I imagine that she would say, “it is impossible that this man should undertake such an affair with any other confidence than what he places in the prudence and skill which he is master of: for that the Grecians have nothing else worthy of account.” Because if she was to hear further, that this same Alcibiades in the first place had not completed the twentieth year of his age; in the next place that he was utterly uninstructed; and besides this, that, when a friend of his advised him first to acquire the knowledge, the prudence, and the habits, necessary for the execution

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: of his designs, before he offered to attack the king, he refused to hearken to this advice, and said, that even in his present condition he was prepared sufficiently; I believe she would be astonished, and would ask, “What kind of a thing it could be then in which the youth put his confidence?” Upon this, were we to tell her, “In his handsome and fine person, in his birth and family, in his riches, and in the natural faculties of his mind,” she would think us, Alcibiades, out of our senses, when she reflected on all the advantages which her son enjoyed of the same kinds. No less do I imagine

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: that Lampido, daughter of Leotychidas, wife of Archidamus, and mother of Agis, who, all of them in their turns, succeeded to the crown of Sparta, she too would wonder, in reflecting on their greatness, were she told, that you had taken it into your head to make war against her son, so ill instructed as you are. And now do you not think it shameful, if the wives of our enemies consider more prudently for us than we do for ourselves, what sort of persons we ought to be before we venture to attack such enemies? Hearken therefore, my good sir, to the advice which

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: I give you, in agreement with the Delphic inscription, KNOW THYSELF: since your antagonists are to be, not those whom you imagine, but these whom I have told you of: and these you never can excel in any other point than skill and application; in which articles if you are found deficient, you will fail of that reputation and renown, as well with Grecians as Barbarians, which I think you long for with more ardour than any other man does for whatever is the object of his wishes.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Can you teach me then, O Socrates, what sort of application I ought to use? for you seem to be entirely right in all which you have spoken.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Something I have indeed to say upon that subject. But let us enter into a joint consultation, you and I, about the means of becoming,

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: both of us, better men. For when I say, there is a necessity for instruction, I mean it of myself as well as of you: since only one difference there is between you and me.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: What is that?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: He who is my guardian is better and wiser than Pericles, who is yours.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: And who is yours, O Socrates?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: A GOD, O Alcibiades! he who permitted me not before this day to enter into any discourse with you: he it is, on whose dictates to me I rely, when I am bold to say, that you will acquire the renown you long for, by no other means than through me.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: You are in jest, Socrates.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Perhaps so: but I speak the truth however in good earnest when I say that we stand in need of instruction, or rather, that all men want it; but that you and I have very especial need of it.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: In saying that I have need of it, you are not mistaken.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Neither am I, in saying that I myself have.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: What then must we do?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: We must not despair, nor give ourselves up to indolence, my friend.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: By no means, Socrates, does it become us so to do.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Indeed it does not. We must therefore consider of the affair, you and I together. Now then answer to my questions.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: We profess to be desirous of becoming as excellent as possible: do we not?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: We do.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: In what kind of excellence?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: In that certainly which belongs to men of merit.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Of merit in what respect?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: In the management of business and affairs, undoubtedly.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: But what business do you mean? The business of a jockey?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Clearly not.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: For then we should go for instruction to those who understand the management of horses.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Certainly we should.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Do you then mean of a mariner?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: I do not.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: For in that case we should apply to those who understand navigation.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Certainly so.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: But what business or affairs then? and by what sort of men are these affairs managed?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: I mean such affairs as are managed by men of honour and merit amongst the Athenians.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Men of honour and merit do you call such as have understanding, or such as are void of understanding?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Such as have understanding.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: In whatever business a man has understanding, in that has he not merit?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: He has.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And in whatever business he is void of understanding, is he not in that void of merit?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Without doubt.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Whether hath a shoemaker understanding in the business of making shoes?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: He certainly has.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: In this respect therefore he has merit.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: He has.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Well; but is not a shoemaker void of understanding in the business of making clothes?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: No doubt of it.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: In this respect therefore he is void of merit.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: He is so.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: The same man therefore, according to this account, is at the same time void of merit and possessed of merit.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: It appears so.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Would you say, then, that men possessed of merit are at the same time void of merit?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: That cannot be.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: What kind of men then do you mean by the men of merit?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: I mean such as have abilities to govern at Athens.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Not to govern horses, I presume.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: No, certainly.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: But to govern men.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: That is my meaning.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: But what men do you mean? Men who are sick?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: I do not mean these.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Men then who are going a voyage?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: I mean not such men.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Men then who are gathering the harvest?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Nor such neither.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: But men who do nothing do you mean? or men who do something?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Men who do something.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Who do what? try if you can make me sensible of your precise meaning?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Well then. I mean men who have commerce one with another, and make use of one another’s aid and assistance in that kind of life which we lead in cities.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: You speak then of such as have abilities to govern men, who make use of other men to aid and assist them.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: I do.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Do you mean the governing of men who make use of mariners in the rowing of galleys, and give them the proper orders?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: I mean no such thing.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: For ability to govern such men belongs to the commander of a galley.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: True.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Do you then mean the governing of men who are musicians,

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: and lead the song to other men, making use of chorus-singers and dancers?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: I mean not this neither.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: For this skill belongs to the master of the whole choir.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Right.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: In speaking then of ability to govern men who make use of other men, what kind of use do you mean? or in what way?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Fellow-citizens, I mean, partakers of the same polity, and engaged in mutual commerce for mutual help and benefit. I speak of ability to govern these.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: What art then is that which gives this ability? as if I were to ask you, on the subject just now mentioned—the knowing how to govern men embarked in the same voyage—What art is it that gives this knowledge?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: The art of commanding ships.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And what science is that which gives the power of governing those others whom we mentioned,—those who have parts in the same song?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: That which belongs, as just now you said, to the master of the whole choir.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And by what name do you call that science which gives ability to govern those who partake of the same polity?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Prudence I call it for my part, Socrates.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: What? do you think then that want of prudence is proper for the commander of a ship?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Certainly not so.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: But rather that prudence is.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: I think it is, so far as it regards the safety of those who are sailing in the ship.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: It is well said: and that other science, that which you call prudence, what end does that regard?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: The good government and safety of the commonwealth.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And what is it which the commonwealth enjoys when it is governed best and preserved in safety? and what is it from which it is then preserved? as, if you were to ask me this question, What is it which the body enjoys when it is best: taken care of, and preserved in safety? and from what is it then preserved? I would say that then it enjoys health, and is preserved from disease. Are not you of the same opinion?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: I am.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And, if you were to ask me further, What do the eyes enjoy when the best care is taken of them? and from what are they then preserved I would answer in like manner as before, that they enjoyed their sight, and were preserved from blindness. So likewise of the ears; when they are preserved from deafness, and have their hearing perfect, they are then in their best condition, and are taken the best care of.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Right.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Well, now; what does the commonwealth enjoy and from what is it preserved, when ’tis in its best condition, has the best care taken of it, and is best preserved?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: It seems to me, Socrates, that the members of it then enjoy mutual amity, and are preserved from enmity and factions.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: By amity do you mean their being of the same mind, or of different minds?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Their being of the same mind.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Now through what science is it that different civil states are of the same mind concerning numbers?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Through the science of arithmetic.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Well; and is it not through that very science that private persons are of the same mind one with another?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: It is.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And that any person too, by himself, continues always in the same mind, is it not through his possessing that science?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: It is.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And through what science is it that a single individual is always of the same mind

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: concerning a span and a cubit, whether of the two is the greater measure? is it not through the science of mensuration?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Without doubt.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And is it not so too between different private persons and civil states?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: It is.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And how concerning weights? does not the same hold true in this case?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: I agree it does.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: But now the sameness of mind which you speak of, what is that? What is the subject-matter of it? and through what science is it procured? I ask you likewise whether the same science which procures it for the public procures it no less for private persons; and whether it operates that effect in a man considered by himself as well as between one man and an other.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Probably it does.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: What science or art then is it? Do not labour for an answer,

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: but speak readily what you think.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: I think it to be such an amity and sameness of mind, that which we are speaking of, as there is between a father and a mother in loving their child, and as there is between brother and brother, and between man and wife.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Do you then think it possible, Alcibiades, for a man to be of the same mind with his wife on the subject of weaving, when he is ignorant and she is knowing in the art?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: By no means.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Nor ought he neither. For ’tis a piece of knowledge belonging only to women.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Certainly.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Well; and can a woman be of the same mind with her husband on the subject of fighting in battle among the infantry, when she has never learnt the art?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Certainly she cannot.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: For the knowledge of this you would perhaps say belonged only to men.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: I should so.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Some pieces of knowledge, therefore, properly belong to women; others to men according to your account.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: No doubt can be made of it.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: On those subjects therefore which are not common to both the sexes there is no sameness of mind, between husbands and their wives.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: There is not any.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Neither then is there any friendship; if friendship consists in sameness of mind.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: It appears there is not.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: So far therefore as women are attentive to their own business they are not beloved by their husbands.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: It seems they are not.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Neither are men beloved by their wives,—so far as their minds are engaged in their own business.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: It seems they are not.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Neither then do citizens live well together in cities, when each of them minds only his own business.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Nay, Socrates; for my part I imagine that they do,—so far as they are thus employed.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: How say you? What, without friendship between them, by means of which we said that civil states were in a happy condition, and without which we said they could not flourish?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: But it seems to me that friendship is on this very account produced between them, because every one gives his whole attention to his own business.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: It did not seem so to you just now. But how do you explain at present what you said,—that friendship was produced by sameness of mind? Whether is it possible that fellow-citizens can be all of the same mind on subjects in which some of them are knowing, and others ignorant?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: It is not possible.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And do they do their duty, and act as they ought, or not, when each of them attends to his own business?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: As they ought, undoubtedly.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: When the citizens then of any city act as they ought, and all of them do their duty, is not friendship produced between them?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: It must be so I think, Socrates.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: What kind of friendship, or sameness of mind do you then mean,

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: in the procuring of which you say that wisdom and prudence are requisite to make us men of virtue and merit? For I can neither learn from you what it is, nor what objects it regards. But sometimes it seems to regard the same objects, and sometimes not, according to your account of it.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Now by the Gods, Socrates, I know not what I mean myself. But am in danger of appearing to have been, of a long time, in a shameful state of mind, without being sensible of it.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Now therefore you ought to take courage. For if fifty years of your life had elapsed

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: before you had discovered the real state of your mind, an application of it to the care of yourself would have been a difficult task for you. But you are now at the very time of life in which such a discovery should be made, to be of any advantage to you.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: What then am I to do, Socrates, now that I am made sensible of my condition?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Only to answer to the questions I shall put to you, Alcibiades. And if you will so do, you and I, by the favour of God, if any credit may be given to a prophecy of mine, shall both of us be the better for it.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Your prophecy shall be accomplished, as far as the accomplishment depends on my answering to your questions.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Come on then. What is it to take care of oneself?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: That we may not falsely imagine, as we often do, that we are taking care of ourselves, and know not that all the while we are otherwise employed. And when is it that a man is taking that care? Whether when he is taking care of what appertains to him, is he then taking care of himself?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: For my part I must own I think so.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And when is it, think you, that a man is taking care of his feet? whether is it then when he is taking care of the things appertaining to his feet?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: I do not apprehend your meaning.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Do you acknowledge something to be appertaining to the hand,—a ring, for instance? Or does it appertain to any other part of the human body than a finger?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Certainly not.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And does not a shoe appertain to the foot in like manner?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: It does.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Whether then at the time of our taking care of our shoes are we taking care immediately of our feet?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: I do not quite apprehend you, Socrates.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Do you acknowledge that whatever be the subject of our care, a right care of it may be taken?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: I do.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: I ask you then, whether you think that a man takes right care of whatever is the subject of his care, when he improves it and makes it better?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: I answer Yes.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: What art now is that by which our shoes are improved and made better?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: The shoemaker’s art.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: By the shoemaker’s art therefore it is that we take a right care of our shoes.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: True.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And is it also by the shoemaker’s art that we take a right care of our feet? or is it by that art by which we improve our feet and make them better?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: It is by this art.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And do we not improve and make better our feet by the same art by which we improve and make better the rest of our body?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: I believe we do.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And is not this the gymnastic art?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Undoubtedly.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: By the gymnastic art therefore we take care of the foot, and by the shoemaker’s art we take care of what is appertinent to the foot.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Exactly so.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And in like manner by the gymnastic art we take care of our hands, and by the art of engraving rings we take care of what is appertinent to the hand.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Certainly.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: By the gymnastic art also we take care of our bodies; but ’tis by the weaver’s art

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: and some others that we take care of things appertinent to the body.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: I agree with you entirely.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: By one kind of knowledge therefore, we take care of things themselves, and by a different kind of knowledge we take care of things only appertinent to those things which are the principal.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: It appears so.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: You are not therefore taking care of yourself when you are taking care only of the appertinences to yourself.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: At that time ’tis very true I am not.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: For one and the same art, it seems, doth not take care of a thing itself, and of the appertinences to that thing besides.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: It appears to be not the same art.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Now then, by what kind of art might we take care of ourselves?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: I have nothing to answer to this question.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: So much, however, we are agreed in, that it is not an art by which we improve or better any thing which is ours; but an art by which we improve and better our very selves.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: I acknowledge it.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Could we ever know what art would improve or amend a shoe, if we knew not what a shoe was?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Impossible.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Neither could we know what art would make better rings for the finger, if ignorant what a ring for the finger was.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: True.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Well; and can we ever know what art would improve or make a man’s self better, so long as we are ignorant of what we ourselves are?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Impossible.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Let me ask you, then, whether it happens to be an easy thing to know oneself; and whether he was some person of mean attainments in knowledge, he who put up this inscription in the temple at Pytho: or is it a piece of knowledge difficult to be attained and not obvious to every one?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: To me, Socrates, it has often seemed easy and obvious to every one, and often too, at other times, a thing of the greatest difficulty.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: But whether in itself it be an easy thing or not, with respect to us, Alcibiades, the state of the case is this:—had we attained to that piece of knowledge, we should perhaps know what it is to take care of ourselves; but never can we know this so long as we remain ignorant of that.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: These are truths which I acknowledge.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Come then. By what means might it be found what is the very self of every thing? for so we might perhaps find what we ourselves are; but so long as we continue in the dark as to that point, it will be no way possible to know ourselves.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: You are certainly in the right.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Attend now, I conjure you in the name of Jupiter: With whom is it that you are at this present time discoursing? Is it not with me?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: It is.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And am not I discoursing with you?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: You are.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: It is Socrates then, who is discoursing and arguing.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Quite true.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And Alcibiades is attentive to his arguments.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: He is.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Is it not by reason that Socrates thus argues in discourse?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Undoubtedly.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And is not to argue in discourse the same thing as to reason?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Quite the same.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: But is not the person who uses a thing, different from the thing which he uses?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: How do you mean?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: As a shoemaker, for instance, cuts his leather with the sheers, and the paring knife, and other tools.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Well; he does so.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Is not then the shoemaker, who cuts the leather and uses those tools in cutting it, different from the tools which he uses?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Without doubt.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Are not, in like manner, the instruments on which a musician plays, different things from the musician himself?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Certainly.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: It was in this sense that just now I asked you whether you thought that, in all cases, the person who

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: used a thing was different from the thing which he used.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: I think he is.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Now then, to resume the instance of the shoemaker; what say we? does he cut the leather with his tools only, or also with his hands?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: With his hands also.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: He therefore uses also these.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: He does.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And does he not use his eyes also when he is cutting the leather?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: He does.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And we are agreed, that the person who makes use of any things is different from the things which he makes use of.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: We are.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: The shoemaker then, and the musician, are different from

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: the hands and eyes with which they perform their operations.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: It is apparent.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And does not a man use also his whole body?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Most certainly.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Now the user is different from the thing used.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: True.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: A man therefore is a being different from his body.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: It seems so.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: What sort of being then is man?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: I know not.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: But you know that man is some being who makes use of the body.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: True.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Does any being make use of the body other than the soul?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: None other.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And does it not so do by governing the body?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: It does.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Further. I suppose that no man would ever think otherwise than this.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Than what?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: That a man himself was one of these three things.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: What three things?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Soul, or body or a compound of them both, constituting one whole.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: What besides could be imagined?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Now we agreed that the being which governs the body is the man.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: We did.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: What being then is the man? Doth the body itself govern itself?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: By no means.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: For the body we said was governed.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: True.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: The body then cannot be that being which we are in search of.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: It seems not.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: But whether does the compound being govern the body? and whether is this the man?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Perhaps it is.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Least of any of the three can this be so. For of two parties, one of which is the party governed, there is no possibility that both of them should govern jointly.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Right.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Since then neither the body, nor the compound of soul and body together, is the man, it remains, I think, either that a man’s self is nothing at all, or if it be any thing, it must be concluded that the man is no other thing than soul.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Clearly so.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Needs it then to be proved to you still more clearly, that the soul is the very man?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: It needs not, by Jupiter: for the proofs already brought seem to me sufficient.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: If it be proved tolerably well, though not accurately, ’tis sufficient for us. For we shall then perhaps, and not before, have an accurate knowledge of man’s self,

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: when we shall have discovered what we just now passed by as a matter which required much consideration.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: What is that?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: That of which was said some such thing as this,—that in the first place we should consider what is self itself: whereas, instead of this, we have been considering what is the proper self of every man. And this indeed for our purpose will perhaps suffice. For we could by no means ever say that any thing was more peculiarly and properly oneself, than is the soul.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Certainly, we could not.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: May we not then fairly thus determine,—that we are converting one with another, by means of reason, you and I, soul with soul?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Quite fairly.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: This therefore was our meaning when we said a little before, that Socrates discoursed with Alcibiades, making use of reason: we meant, it seems, that he directed his words and arguments, not to your outward person, but to Alcibiades himself, that is to the soul.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: It seems so to me too.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: He therefore enjoins a man to recognize the soul, he who gives him this injunction,—to know himself.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: That is probably his meaning.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Whoever then has a knowledge only of his body, has indeed attained the knowledge of what is his, but not the knowledge of himself.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Just so.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: None therefore of the physicians, so far as he is only a physician, knows himself: neither does any master of the exercises, so far as he is such a master and nothing more.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: It seems they do not.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Far from knowing themselves then are husbandmen, and other artificers or workmen. For such men as these are ignorant it seems of the things which are theirs, and knowing only in subjects still more remote, the mere appertinences to those things which are theirs, so far as their several arts lead them. For they are acquainted

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: only with things appertinent to the body, to the culture and service of which body these things administer.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: What you say is true.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: If therefore wisdom consist in the knowledge of oneself, none of these artificers are wise men by their skill in their respective arts.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: I think they are not.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: On this account it is that these arts seem mechanical and mean, and not the learning fit for a man of a virtuous merit.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Entirely true.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: To return to our subject, whoever then employs his care in the service of his body, takes care indeed of what is his, but not of himself.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: There is danger of its being found so.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And whoever is attentive to the improvement of his wealth, is not taking care either of himself

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: or of what is his, but of things still more remote, the mere appertinences to what is his.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: It seems so to me too.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: The man therefore who is intent on getting money, is so far not acting for his own advantage.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Rightly concluded.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: It follows also, that whoever was an admirer of the outward person of Alcibiades, did not admire Alcibiades, but something which belongs to Alcibiades.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: You say what is true.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: But whoever is your admirer is the admirer of your soul.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: It appears to follow of necessity from our reasoning.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And hence it is, that the admirer of your outward person, when the flower of it is all fallen, departs and forsakes you.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: So it appears.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: But the admirer of a soul departs not, so long as that soul goes on to improve itself.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Probably so.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: I am he then who forsakes you not, but abides by you, when the flower of youth having left you, the rest of your followers have left you and are gone.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: It is kindly done of you, Socrates: and never do you forsake me.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Exert all your endeavours then to be as excellent a man as possible.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: I will do my best.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: For the state of your case is this:—Alcibiades,

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: the son of Clinias; never it seems had any admirer, neither has he now, besides one only, and therefore to be cherished, this Socrates here, the son of Sophroniscus and Phænarete.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: ’Tis true.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Did you not say that I had been a little beforehand with you when accosted you; for that you had it in your mind to address me first; as you wanted to ask me, why of all your admirers I was the only one who forsook you not?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: I did say so: and that was the very case.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: This then was the reason: ’twas because I was the only person who admired you; the others admired that which is yours. That which is yours has already dropped its flower;

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: and the spring-season of it is past: whereas you yourself are but beginning to flourish. If therefore the Athenian populace corrupt you not, and make you less fair, I never shall forsake you. But this is what I chiefly fear, that you may come to admire and court the populace, and be corrupted by them, and we should lose you: since many of the Athenians, men of virtuous merit too, have been thus corrupted before now. For the people of magnanimous Erectheus has an outward person fair and engaging to behold. But we ought to strip it of all its showy dress, and view it naked. Use therefore the caution which I give you.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: What caution?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: In the first place, my friend, exercise yourself; and acquire the knowledge of those things which are necessary to be learnt by every man who engages in political affairs: but engage not in them until you are thus exercised and thus instructed: that you may come to them prepared with an antidote, and suffer no harm from the poison of the populace.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: What you say, Socrates, to me seems right. But explain, if you can, more clearly, how or in what way we should take care of ourselves.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Is not this then sufficiently clear to us from what has been already said? For what we are, has been tolerably well agreed on. Indeed before that point was settled we feared lest we should mistake it, and imagine that we were taking care of ourselves, when the object of our care all the while was some other thing.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: This is true.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Upon that it was concluded by both of us that we ought to take care of the soul, and that to this we should direct all our attention and regard.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: It was evident.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: And that the care of our bodies and our possessions should be delivered over to others.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: We could not doubt it.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: In what way then may we attain to know the soul itself with the greatest dearness? For, when we know this, it seems we shall know ourselves. Now, in the name of the Gods, whether are we not ignorant of the right meaning of that Delphic inscription just now mentioned?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: What meaning? What have you in your thoughts, O Socrates! when you ask this question?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: I will tell you what I suspect that this inscription means, and what particular thing it advises us to do. For a just resemblance of it is, I think, not to be found wherever one pleases; but in one only thing, the fight.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: How do you mean?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: Consider it jointly now with me. Were a man to address himself to the outward human eye, as if it were some other man; and were he to give it this counsel “See yourself;” what particular thing should we suppose that he advised the eye to do? Should we not suppose that ’twas to look at such a thing, as that the eye, by looking at it, might see itself?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: Certainly we should.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: What kind of thing then do we think of, by looking at which

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: we see the thing at which we look, and at the same time see our selves?

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: ALCIBIADES: ’Tis evident, O Socrates, that for this purpose we must look at mirrors, and other things of the like kind.

segments.heading: The First Alcibiades
segments.text: SOCRATES: You are right. And has not the eye itself, with which we see, something of the same kind belonging to it?
